Only for non-sensitive information Enables users to generate, edit, and enhance images, videos, and 3D content from text prompts. Payment/support label: Paid ( Procurement purchase required ). This listing does not establish coursework or examination permission.

LumaLabs AI is listed in UChicago’s approved/restricted table under these data and purpose conditions: Approved up to SRDS low protection level.. Only for non-sensitive information Generates and edits images, videos, audio, and text from natural language prompts Payment/support label: Paid ( Procurement purchase required ). This listing does not establish coursework or examination permission.
Whether AI writing and research tools constitute academic dishonesty depends on the instructor of record’s rules. Students should address doubts about appropriate use to that instructor.
UChicago student guidance requires students to follow the instructor’s rules on when and how AI may be used in coursework. Course policies may differ; students should ask when unclear.

UChicago student guidance states that AI use without proper attribution breaches academic integrity. Its detailed guidance calls for acknowledging AI assistance when appropriate; attribution does not override instructor or unit prohibitions.

Law School §4.9 covers generative and agentic functions, including embedded tools and multi-agent systems. Basic error correction and source search/retrieval are excluded, but substantive rewriting and generated synthesis count as AI.
Law School generative AI use is prohibited during exams by default unless the instructor specifies otherwise. The default does not prohibit compliant use while studying for an exam.

Under the Law School default, AI use in submitted work is compared to unattributed use of a human author’s work. Some uses such as brainstorming or proofreading can comply; AI composing all or part of a paper violates the default even with attribution.
Law School instructors may set different AI policies. Deviations from the default must be stated in writing in the syllabus posted on Canvas.
Within BSD PhD and Master’s programs, students should not rely on generative AI for graded coursework or examinations unless the instructor, program or committee has approved the use in advance.

BSD thesis/dissertation, capstone and independent-project AI use is subject to mentor, program or committee discretion. Core research, analysis and conclusions must remain the student’s own. Absent specific guidance, use beyond basic language editing requires prior scoped authorization; approved use must be disclosed.

AI cannot be an author on BSD-affiliated scholarly products. AI contributions must be disclosed according to the target venue’s requirements, and AI use in human-subjects protocols must be disclosed to the IRB.

BSD requires enterprise-approved tools for University data and specifically IRB- or data-agreement-approved tools for regulated research data. Public AI tools may be used only with non-sensitive public information; protected student, personal and unpublished/restricted research data require approval for that use.

College guidance recognises AI detectors are imperfect. Instructors and OCCS may use Pangram as supporting information in a transparent, human-led academic integrity process and student conversations; it is not automatic proof of misconduct. Unit policies and instructor choices may differ.

The College disciplinary process must not presume credibility or culpability. OCCS or the relevant committee gathers and evaluates information and determines responsibility by a preponderance of evidence. This is a general procedure, not an automatic AI penalty.

Before a College Area Disciplinary Committee meeting, the student receives the written materials and at least two business days to submit a response. This committee-stage rule must not be confused with other stages or academic units.

College students may bring a support person, who may advise but may not speak for the student or question the subcommittee. Students should notify OCCS three to five business days in advance; for a lawyer, notice should be at least seven business days and University counsel must also attend.

A College student may request review of a committee decision imposing a sanction after a responsibility finding. Review follows the separately referenced University procedures; no unverified deadline or automatic appeal outcome is inferred here.

Harris permits AI coursework assistance only when the course/instructor does not prohibit it, AI supports rather than replaces learning, the specific program is cited and the student checks accuracy. Students should explain use and save original outputs in case requested.

Harris requires citation of the specific AI program used. Students should explain how AI was used and save full original generated text in case requested; failure to cite AI use constitutes academic dishonesty.

Harris disciplinary probation entails specified restrictions on emergency scholarship funding and Career Development/HarrisLink services, permanent ineligibility for on-campus academic jobs such as TA/proctor, and loss of good standing. Further violations during probation are referred to the Area committee. These are general sanction consequences, not automatic penalties for AI use.
PhoenixAI users are responsible for citing generated content used in papers, presentations, course assignments or publications. Service access and citation do not override assessment restrictions.
PhoenixAI is intended for education, research and professional development; commercial use is prohibited.

UChicago reserves the right to monitor PhoenixAI for compliance, subject to its account-privacy policy. Noncompliance may lead to restricted access or other disciplinary action; this does not establish unrestricted monitoring or a fixed AI penalty.
CCRF prohibits materials prepared with generative AI assistance, expressly including Phoenix AI, in its undergraduate research and national fellowships applications.
History faculty specify classroom AI policies in the syllabus. In the absence of a syllabus statement, the departmental assumption is that generative AI use in the class is prohibited.
History faculty and instructors will refrain from using generative AI to grade student assignments.

UChicago’s general guidance prohibits vendors from training or improving models with University data. The Workspace Studio table separately warns that data may be shared for training unless users opt out. Both statements are retained; automatic activation is not evidence of permission to enable training, and the University’s reconciliation remains unverified.

Academic units have their own written disciplinary procedures; the central Area page provides a general outline. College students must use the separately published College process and Harris students must check Harris rules. General sanctions do not establish an automatic penalty for AI use.

Under the general Area process, where a student acknowledges responsibility and warning/probation is the likely outcome, the Dean may offer administrative resolution. The student may accept or reject in writing; acceptance is final and unreviewable within the University except if new material information leads to withdrawal and committee referral. This is not an automatic AI penalty.

Under the general Area sanctions framework, only the Area Disciplinary Committee may suspend or expel a student; it may recommend revocation for misconduct before degree conferral. These are possible general sanctions, not fixed AI-use penalties or College-specific procedural deadlines.

The University of Chicago maintains a page listing approved, restricted, and unauthorized AI tools, with use conditions and review information for the university community.

Use of confidential data with publicly available GenAI tools is prohibited without prior security and privacy review. This includes personally identifiable employee, FERPA-covered student and HIPAA-covered patient data, and may include research that is not yet publicly available.

At the University of Chicago, generative AI systems, applications, and software products that process, analyze, or move confidential data require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free.
At the University of Chicago, use of University data by vendors to train or improve their AI models is not permitted.

At the University of Chicago, confidential, sensitive, or restricted data should not be used with generative AI tools unless the tool and the use have been reviewed and approved through the appropriate University process.

At the University of Chicago, even when an AI tool is listed as approved, it is not risk-free. Approval means the tool can be used under specific conditions, but users are still responsible for evaluating the sensitivity of their data and ensuring confidential, regulated, or contract-restricted information is not shared unless explicitly allowed.

UChicago lists PhoenixAI for general use, with sensitive-information use subject to IRB approval. Separate PhoenixAI service terms govern citation, non-commercial use, monitoring and possible access restrictions or disciplinary action.
At the University of Chicago, ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4.0 are approved only for data that is made publicly available by its source, with restrictions limiting use to non-sensitive information.
At the University of Chicago, AI-generated content may be misleading or inaccurate, and it is the responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content.

At the University of Chicago, if a proposed AI tool use exceeds standard risk tolerance but is not prohibited by compliance regulations, a Risk Acceptance Letter may be prepared to document reviewed and accepted risks under specific conditions.
The University of Chicago provides a central hub at genai.uchicago.edu for information on generative AI tools, training, resources, and guidance for the university community.

UChicago’s AI policy crosswalk states, in its staff Business Conduct context, that AI transcription or assistant tools may not secretly record or join meetings; AI use must protect confidential data. The underlying Business Conduct Policy was not independently obtained.

At the University of Chicago, AI tools may not be used to generate harassing, discriminatory, or otherwise unlawful content, including the use of AI to create or alter images, audio, and videos, per the Policy on Harassment, Discrimination, and Sexual Misconduct.

At the University of Chicago, entering sensitive data into AI tools without review and approval by security, privacy, and the appropriate data steward may create an unauthorized data disclosure that may violate University policy, federal and state law, sponsor or contract obligations, and data use agreements.

UChicago student guidance requires students to follow the instructor’s rules on when and how AI may be used in coursework. Course policies may differ; students should ask when unclear.

UChicago student guidance states that AI use without proper attribution breaches academic integrity. Its detailed guidance calls for acknowledging AI assistance when appropriate; attribution does not override instructor or unit prohibitions.

Law School §4.9 covers generative and agentic functions, including embedded tools and multi-agent systems. Basic error correction and source search/retrieval are excluded, but substantive rewriting and generated synthesis count as AI.
Law School generative AI use is prohibited during exams by default unless the instructor specifies otherwise. The default does not prohibit compliant use while studying for an exam.

Under the Law School default, AI use in submitted work is compared to unattributed use of a human author’s work. Some uses such as brainstorming or proofreading can comply; AI composing all or part of a paper violates the default even with attribution.
Law School instructors may set different AI policies. Deviations from the default must be stated in writing in the syllabus posted on Canvas.
Within BSD PhD and Master’s programs, students should not rely on generative AI for graded coursework or examinations unless the instructor, program or committee has approved the use in advance.

BSD thesis/dissertation, capstone and independent-project AI use is subject to mentor, program or committee discretion. Core research, analysis and conclusions must remain the student’s own. Absent specific guidance, use beyond basic language editing requires prior scoped authorization; approved use must be disclosed.

AI cannot be an author on BSD-affiliated scholarly products. AI contributions must be disclosed according to the target venue’s requirements, and AI use in human-subjects protocols must be disclosed to the IRB.

BSD requires enterprise-approved tools for University data and specifically IRB- or data-agreement-approved tools for regulated research data. Public AI tools may be used only with non-sensitive public information; protected student, personal and unpublished/restricted research data require approval for that use.

College guidance recognises AI detectors are imperfect. Instructors and OCCS may use Pangram as supporting information in a transparent, human-led academic integrity process and student conversations; it is not automatic proof of misconduct. Unit policies and instructor choices may differ.

The College disciplinary process must not presume credibility or culpability. OCCS or the relevant committee gathers and evaluates information and determines responsibility by a preponderance of evidence. This is a general procedure, not an automatic AI penalty.

Before a College Area Disciplinary Committee meeting, the student receives the written materials and at least two business days to submit a response. This committee-stage rule must not be confused with other stages or academic units.

College students may bring a support person, who may advise but may not speak for the student or question the subcommittee. Students should notify OCCS three to five business days in advance; for a lawyer, notice should be at least seven business days and University counsel must also attend.

A College student may request review of a committee decision imposing a sanction after a responsibility finding. Review follows the separately referenced University procedures; no unverified deadline or automatic appeal outcome is inferred here.

Harris permits AI coursework assistance only when the course/instructor does not prohibit it, AI supports rather than replaces learning, the specific program is cited and the student checks accuracy. Students should explain use and save original outputs in case requested.

Harris requires citation of the specific AI program used. Students should explain how AI was used and save full original generated text in case requested; failure to cite AI use constitutes academic dishonesty.

Harris disciplinary probation entails specified restrictions on emergency scholarship funding and Career Development/HarrisLink services, permanent ineligibility for on-campus academic jobs such as TA/proctor, and loss of good standing. Further violations during probation are referred to the Area committee. These are general sanction consequences, not automatic penalties for AI use.
PhoenixAI users are responsible for citing generated content used in papers, presentations, course assignments or publications. Service access and citation do not override assessment restrictions.
PhoenixAI is intended for education, research and professional development; commercial use is prohibited.

UChicago reserves the right to monitor PhoenixAI for compliance, subject to its account-privacy policy. Noncompliance may lead to restricted access or other disciplinary action; this does not establish unrestricted monitoring or a fixed AI penalty.
CCRF prohibits materials prepared with generative AI assistance, expressly including Phoenix AI, in its undergraduate research and national fellowships applications.
History faculty specify classroom AI policies in the syllabus. In the absence of a syllabus statement, the departmental assumption is that generative AI use in the class is prohibited.
History faculty and instructors will refrain from using generative AI to grade student assignments.

UChicago’s general guidance prohibits vendors from training or improving models with University data. The Workspace Studio table separately warns that data may be shared for training unless users opt out. Both statements are retained; automatic activation is not evidence of permission to enable training, and the University’s reconciliation remains unverified.

Academic units have their own written disciplinary procedures; the central Area page provides a general outline. College students must use the separately published College process and Harris students must check Harris rules. General sanctions do not establish an automatic penalty for AI use.

Under the general Area process, where a student acknowledges responsibility and warning/probation is the likely outcome, the Dean may offer administrative resolution. The student may accept or reject in writing; acceptance is final and unreviewable within the University except if new material information leads to withdrawal and committee referral. This is not an automatic AI penalty.

Under the general Area sanctions framework, only the Area Disciplinary Committee may suspend or expel a student; it may recommend revocation for misconduct before degree conferral. These are possible general sanctions, not fixed AI-use penalties or College-specific procedural deadlines.

At the University of Chicago, if a proposed AI tool use exceeds standard risk tolerance but is not prohibited by compliance regulations, a Risk Acceptance Letter may be prepared to document reviewed and accepted risks under specific conditions.

At the University of Chicago, use of confidential data with publicly available generative AI tools is prohibited without prior security and privacy review. This includes personally identifiable employee data, FERPA-covered student data, HIPAA-covered patient data, and research that is not yet publicly available.

At the University of Chicago, generative AI systems, applications, and software products that process, analyze, or move confidential data require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free.
At the University of Chicago, use of University data by vendors to train or improve their AI models is not permitted.

At the University of Chicago, confidential, sensitive, or restricted data should not be used with generative AI tools unless the tool and the use have been reviewed and approved through the appropriate University process.

At the University of Chicago, even when an AI tool is listed as approved, it is not risk-free. Approval means the tool can be used under specific conditions, but users are still responsible for evaluating the sensitivity of their data and ensuring confidential, regulated, or contract-restricted information is not shared unless explicitly allowed.
At the University of Chicago, PhoenixAI is the university's internal generative AI platform, approved for general use and can be used for sensitive information with IRB approval.
At the University of Chicago, ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4.0 are approved only for data that is made publicly available by its source, with restrictions limiting use to non-sensitive information.
At the University of Chicago, AI-generated content may be misleading or inaccurate, and it is the responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content.
The University of Chicago provides a central hub at genai.uchicago.edu for information on generative AI tools, training, resources, and guidance for the university community.
At the University of Chicago, AI transcription or assistant tools may not be used to secretly record or join meetings, per the Business Conduct Policy.

At the University of Chicago, AI tools may not be used to generate harassing, discriminatory, or otherwise unlawful content, including the use of AI to create or alter images, audio, and videos, per the Policy on Harassment, Discrimination, and Sexual Misconduct.

At the University of Chicago, entering sensitive data into AI tools without review and approval by security, privacy, and the appropriate data steward may create an unauthorized data disclosure that may violate University policy, federal and state law, sponsor or contract obligations, and data use agreements.

The University of Chicago maintains a page listing approved, restricted, and unauthorized AI tools, with use conditions and review information for the university community.

At the University of Chicago, if a proposed AI tool use exceeds standard risk tolerance but is not prohibited by compliance regulations, a Risk Acceptance Letter may be prepared to document reviewed and accepted risks under specific conditions.

At the University of Chicago, use of confidential data with publicly available generative AI tools is prohibited without prior security and privacy review. This includes personally identifiable employee data, FERPA-covered student data, HIPAA-covered patient data, and research that is not yet publicly available.

At the University of Chicago, generative AI systems, applications, and software products that process, analyze, or move confidential data require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free.
At the University of Chicago, use of University data by vendors to train or improve their AI models is not permitted.

At the University of Chicago, confidential, sensitive, or restricted data should not be used with generative AI tools unless the tool and the use have been reviewed and approved through the appropriate University process.

At the University of Chicago, even when an AI tool is listed as approved, it is not risk-free. Approval means the tool can be used under specific conditions, but users are still responsible for evaluating the sensitivity of their data and ensuring confidential, regulated, or contract-restricted information is not shared unless explicitly allowed.
At the University of Chicago, PhoenixAI is the university's internal generative AI platform, approved for general use and can be used for sensitive information with IRB approval.
At the University of Chicago, ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4.0 are approved only for data that is made publicly available by its source, with restrictions limiting use to non-sensitive information.
At the University of Chicago, AI-generated content may be misleading or inaccurate, and it is the responsibility of the tool user to review the accuracy and ownership of any AI-generated content.
The University of Chicago provides a central hub at genai.uchicago.edu for information on generative AI tools, training, resources, and guidance for the university community.
At the University of Chicago, AI transcription or assistant tools may not be used to secretly record or join meetings, per the Business Conduct Policy.

At the University of Chicago, AI tools may not be used to generate harassing, discriminatory, or otherwise unlawful content, including the use of AI to create or alter images, audio, and videos, per the Policy on Harassment, Discrimination, and Sexual Misconduct.

At the University of Chicago, entering sensitive data into AI tools without review and approval by security, privacy, and the appropriate data steward may create an unauthorized data disclosure that may violate University policy, federal and state law, sponsor or contract obligations, and data use agreements.

Peking University's AI Scientific Integrity Platform defines AI use boundaries across seven research stages: topic selection, literature search and management, research design and implementation, paper writing, paper submission, paper review, and grant application and review.
Peking University's AI use guidelines apply to faculty, students, researchers, and administrators who use generative AI or other AI-assisted tools in teaching, research, and management activities.

Peking University classifies AI use in research into three tiers: open use (low risk, broadly applicable), limited use (moderate risk, requires verification and constraints), and prohibited use (high risk or violation, forbidden).

Peking University distinguishes two levels of AI involvement in research: instrumental assistance (using AI as a tool to handle routine or repetitive tasks) and replacement completion (using AI to independently complete tasks involving core intellectual contribution and creative labor).

Peking University's AI Scientific Integrity Platform synthesizes AI use policies from 18 domestic and international sources, including Chinese government agencies (MOST, NSFC), Chinese universities (Fudan, Nanjing, Sichuan), international bodies (EU Commission, NIH), and universities (Harvard, Yale, Cambridge, UCL, Oxford, MIT).

claimChanges.claimText: Claude Anthropic is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn’s Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) maintains updated institutional guidance on Penn-licensed AI tools, providing community access to PennChat (with free daily token allotments for FERPA-protected educational records and HIPAA-protected health information via PennKey while on campus or VPN), alongside Anthropic Enterprise (Claude), Articulate AI Assistant, Adobe Express, and Copilot Chat, while mandating that instructors must not require students to enter personal information or intellectual property into unlicensed tools.

Penn's Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) instructs faculty that in all cases they should not upload student work into AI detectors, stating that uploading student work without consent violates FERPA and Penn privacy policies, and noting that AI detectors are not accurate enough to serve as evidence of misconduct due to frequent bias.

Google NotebookLM is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft M365 Copilot (Premium) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft Copilot Chat (Basic) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Snowflake Data Analytics Platform & Consulting is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.
PennChat (Pilot) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Grammarly for Education is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Gemini for Google Workspace is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

ChatGPT Edu is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn's CETLI generative AI guidance page was updated from referring to 'Penn AI Guidance and Policies' to 'Penn AI Tools and Policies', adding that Penn offers access to AI tools and provides policies to help instructors and staff determine which tools are acceptable for different types of student data.

Penn requires all community members (educators, staff, researchers, and students) to be transparent about the use of AI and to disclose when a work product was created wholly or partially using an AI tool.

Penn provides several licensed AI tools to its community, including Copilot Chat (Basic, free), Adobe Express (free), ChatGPT-EDU (purchase required), M365 Copilot Premium (purchase required), Gemini for Google Workspace (purchase required), Google NotebookLM (purchase required), Grammarly Pro (purchase required), Snowflake Data Analytics (purchase required), and Zoom AI Companion (free).
Users of AI at Penn are accountable for AI-generated content and should validate its accuracy with trusted first-party sources, being wary of misinformation or hallucinations.

Penn users should not input moderate or high-risk Penn data (per the Penn Data Risk Classification) or intellectual property into AI tools without careful consideration of data use policies, a protective contract, and review by Penn's Privacy Office and Office of Information Security.

It is not permissible under HIPAA or Penn Medicine policy to share patient or research participant information with open or public AI tools and services such as ChatGPT; individual patient data and data sets (even if deidentified) may not be exposed to such tools absent institutional approval.

Penn researchers should obtain IRB approvals prior to exposing research participant data to AI tools and should exercise caution when research involves high-risk data including PII and health information.

Penn's Office of Audit, Compliance & Privacy mandates that users of publicly available (unlicensed) AI tools must not enter any information that could identify a student, including names, ID numbers, email addresses, or detailed descriptions of student work or engagement that could be identifiable to others.

Penn mandates that student work (papers, projects) must not be entered into unlicensed AI tools without the student's permission, even if anonymized, because this work is part of the student's confidential academic record.

Instructors must not require students to enter their own work into unlicensed AI tools or use such tools in assignments; unlicensed tools may be used optionally by students at the instructor's discretion, but Penn-licensed tools should be used for mandatory coursework components.
Individual instructors at Penn determine their own policies related to acceptable student use of generative AI in coursework.

Penn community members should avoid uploading confidential or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize intellectual property rights.
University business processes using AI should have oversight, review, and verification of AI outputs in place to ensure reliability, consistency, and accuracy.

Penn educators should provide students with clear guidelines on the use of AI within coursework and should disclose to students when course materials have been created with AI or when AI detection software will be used.

In the absence of other guidance, Penn students should treat the use of AI as they would treat assistance from another person — if it is unacceptable to have another person substantially complete a task like writing an essay, it is also unacceptable to have AI complete the task.
Penn researchers should consult with department leadership and their discipline's publishing standards to determine how AI use should be accounted for with regard to authorship in publications.

At Wharton Academy, AI-generated work should be cited like any other reference material, including how and where students used AI-generated information; using AI-generated work without crediting the source is considered plagiarism.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from using AI to complete personal reflection or opinion-based tasks, from using AI to complete group assignments instead of collaborating with peers, and from using AI to cheat on exams or tests.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from directly copying answers from generative AI tools and submitting them as their own, from using AI to paraphrase or rewrite plagiarized content, and from posting AI-generated discussion posts within course community forums.

Wharton Academy permits students to use generative AI for brainstorming, learning efficiency, getting prompts, exploring different perspectives, asking for templates, getting preliminary feedback on written work, and language translation, at the discretion of faculty and instructional teams.

claimChanges.claimText: Claude Anthropic is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn’s Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) maintains updated institutional guidance on Penn-licensed AI tools, providing community access to PennChat (with free daily token allotments for FERPA-protected educational records and HIPAA-protected health information via PennKey while on campus or VPN), alongside Anthropic Enterprise (Claude), Articulate AI Assistant, Adobe Express, and Copilot Chat, while mandating that instructors must not require students to enter personal information or intellectual property into unlicensed tools.

Penn's Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) instructs faculty that in all cases they should not upload student work into AI detectors, stating that uploading student work without consent violates FERPA and Penn privacy policies, and noting that AI detectors are not accurate enough to serve as evidence of misconduct due to frequent bias.

Microsoft Copilot Chat (Basic) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Snowflake Data Analytics Platform & Consulting is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.
PennChat (Pilot) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Grammarly for Education is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Gemini for Google Workspace is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

ChatGPT Edu is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn's CETLI generative AI guidance page was updated from referring to 'Penn AI Guidance and Policies' to 'Penn AI Tools and Policies', adding that Penn offers access to AI tools and provides policies to help instructors and staff determine which tools are acceptable for different types of student data.

Penn requires all community members (educators, staff, researchers, and students) to be transparent about the use of AI and to disclose when a work product was created wholly or partially using an AI tool.

Penn provides several licensed AI tools to its community, including Copilot Chat (Basic, free), Adobe Express (free), ChatGPT-EDU (purchase required), M365 Copilot Premium (purchase required), Gemini for Google Workspace (purchase required), Google NotebookLM (purchase required), Grammarly Pro (purchase required), Snowflake Data Analytics (purchase required), and Zoom AI Companion (free).
Users of AI at Penn are accountable for AI-generated content and should validate its accuracy with trusted first-party sources, being wary of misinformation or hallucinations.

Penn users should not input moderate or high-risk Penn data (per the Penn Data Risk Classification) or intellectual property into AI tools without careful consideration of data use policies, a protective contract, and review by Penn's Privacy Office and Office of Information Security.

It is not permissible under HIPAA or Penn Medicine policy to share patient or research participant information with open or public AI tools and services such as ChatGPT; individual patient data and data sets (even if deidentified) may not be exposed to such tools absent institutional approval.

Penn researchers should obtain IRB approvals prior to exposing research participant data to AI tools and should exercise caution when research involves high-risk data including PII and health information.

Penn's Office of Audit, Compliance & Privacy mandates that users of publicly available (unlicensed) AI tools must not enter any information that could identify a student, including names, ID numbers, email addresses, or detailed descriptions of student work or engagement that could be identifiable to others.

Penn mandates that student work (papers, projects) must not be entered into unlicensed AI tools without the student's permission, even if anonymized, because this work is part of the student's confidential academic record.

Instructors must not require students to enter their own work into unlicensed AI tools or use such tools in assignments; unlicensed tools may be used optionally by students at the instructor's discretion, but Penn-licensed tools should be used for mandatory coursework components.
Individual instructors at Penn determine their own policies related to acceptable student use of generative AI in coursework.

Penn community members should avoid uploading confidential or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize intellectual property rights.
University business processes using AI should have oversight, review, and verification of AI outputs in place to ensure reliability, consistency, and accuracy.

Penn educators should provide students with clear guidelines on the use of AI within coursework and should disclose to students when course materials have been created with AI or when AI detection software will be used.

In the absence of other guidance, Penn students should treat the use of AI as they would treat assistance from another person — if it is unacceptable to have another person substantially complete a task like writing an essay, it is also unacceptable to have AI complete the task.
Penn researchers should consult with department leadership and their discipline's publishing standards to determine how AI use should be accounted for with regard to authorship in publications.

At Wharton Academy, AI-generated work should be cited like any other reference material, including how and where students used AI-generated information; using AI-generated work without crediting the source is considered plagiarism.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from using AI to complete personal reflection or opinion-based tasks, from using AI to complete group assignments instead of collaborating with peers, and from using AI to cheat on exams or tests.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from directly copying answers from generative AI tools and submitting them as their own, from using AI to paraphrase or rewrite plagiarized content, and from posting AI-generated discussion posts within course community forums.

Wharton Academy permits students to use generative AI for brainstorming, learning efficiency, getting prompts, exploring different perspectives, asking for templates, getting preliminary feedback on written work, and language translation, at the discretion of faculty and instructional teams.

claimChanges.claimText: Claude Anthropic is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn’s Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) maintains updated institutional guidance on Penn-licensed AI tools, providing community access to PennChat (with free daily token allotments for FERPA-protected educational records and HIPAA-protected health information via PennKey while on campus or VPN), alongside Anthropic Enterprise (Claude), Articulate AI Assistant, Adobe Express, and Copilot Chat, while mandating that instructors must not require students to enter personal information or intellectual property into unlicensed tools.

Penn's Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) instructs faculty that in all cases they should not upload student work into AI detectors, stating that uploading student work without consent violates FERPA and Penn privacy policies, and noting that AI detectors are not accurate enough to serve as evidence of misconduct due to frequent bias.

Google NotebookLM is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft M365 Copilot (Premium) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft Copilot Chat (Basic) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Snowflake Data Analytics Platform & Consulting is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.
PennChat (Pilot) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Grammarly for Education is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Gemini for Google Workspace is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

ChatGPT Edu is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn's CETLI generative AI guidance page was updated from referring to 'Penn AI Guidance and Policies' to 'Penn AI Tools and Policies', adding that Penn offers access to AI tools and provides policies to help instructors and staff determine which tools are acceptable for different types of student data.

Penn requires all community members (educators, staff, researchers, and students) to be transparent about the use of AI and to disclose when a work product was created wholly or partially using an AI tool.

Penn provides several licensed AI tools to its community, including Copilot Chat (Basic, free), Adobe Express (free), ChatGPT-EDU (purchase required), M365 Copilot Premium (purchase required), Gemini for Google Workspace (purchase required), Google NotebookLM (purchase required), Grammarly Pro (purchase required), Snowflake Data Analytics (purchase required), and Zoom AI Companion (free).
Users of AI at Penn are accountable for AI-generated content and should validate its accuracy with trusted first-party sources, being wary of misinformation or hallucinations.

Penn users should not input moderate or high-risk Penn data (per the Penn Data Risk Classification) or intellectual property into AI tools without careful consideration of data use policies, a protective contract, and review by Penn's Privacy Office and Office of Information Security.

It is not permissible under HIPAA or Penn Medicine policy to share patient or research participant information with open or public AI tools and services such as ChatGPT; individual patient data and data sets (even if deidentified) may not be exposed to such tools absent institutional approval.

Penn researchers should obtain IRB approvals prior to exposing research participant data to AI tools and should exercise caution when research involves high-risk data including PII and health information.

Penn's Office of Audit, Compliance & Privacy mandates that users of publicly available (unlicensed) AI tools must not enter any information that could identify a student, including names, ID numbers, email addresses, or detailed descriptions of student work or engagement that could be identifiable to others.

Penn mandates that student work (papers, projects) must not be entered into unlicensed AI tools without the student's permission, even if anonymized, because this work is part of the student's confidential academic record.

Instructors must not require students to enter their own work into unlicensed AI tools or use such tools in assignments; unlicensed tools may be used optionally by students at the instructor's discretion, but Penn-licensed tools should be used for mandatory coursework components.
Individual instructors at Penn determine their own policies related to acceptable student use of generative AI in coursework.

Penn community members should avoid uploading confidential or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize intellectual property rights.
University business processes using AI should have oversight, review, and verification of AI outputs in place to ensure reliability, consistency, and accuracy.

Penn educators should provide students with clear guidelines on the use of AI within coursework and should disclose to students when course materials have been created with AI or when AI detection software will be used.

In the absence of other guidance, Penn students should treat the use of AI as they would treat assistance from another person — if it is unacceptable to have another person substantially complete a task like writing an essay, it is also unacceptable to have AI complete the task.
Penn researchers should consult with department leadership and their discipline's publishing standards to determine how AI use should be accounted for with regard to authorship in publications.

At Wharton Academy, AI-generated work should be cited like any other reference material, including how and where students used AI-generated information; using AI-generated work without crediting the source is considered plagiarism.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from using AI to complete personal reflection or opinion-based tasks, from using AI to complete group assignments instead of collaborating with peers, and from using AI to cheat on exams or tests.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from directly copying answers from generative AI tools and submitting them as their own, from using AI to paraphrase or rewrite plagiarized content, and from posting AI-generated discussion posts within course community forums.

Wharton Academy permits students to use generative AI for brainstorming, learning efficiency, getting prompts, exploring different perspectives, asking for templates, getting preliminary feedback on written work, and language translation, at the discretion of faculty and instructional teams.

claimChanges.claimText: Claude Anthropic is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn’s Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) maintains updated institutional guidance on Penn-licensed AI tools, providing community access to PennChat (with free daily token allotments for FERPA-protected educational records and HIPAA-protected health information via PennKey while on campus or VPN), alongside Anthropic Enterprise (Claude), Articulate AI Assistant, Adobe Express, and Copilot Chat, while mandating that instructors must not require students to enter personal information or intellectual property into unlicensed tools.

Penn's Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) instructs faculty that in all cases they should not upload student work into AI detectors, stating that uploading student work without consent violates FERPA and Penn privacy policies, and noting that AI detectors are not accurate enough to serve as evidence of misconduct due to frequent bias.

Google NotebookLM is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft M365 Copilot (Premium) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft Copilot Chat (Basic) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Snowflake Data Analytics Platform & Consulting is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.
PennChat (Pilot) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Grammarly for Education is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Gemini for Google Workspace is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

ChatGPT Edu is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn's CETLI generative AI guidance page was updated from referring to 'Penn AI Guidance and Policies' to 'Penn AI Tools and Policies', adding that Penn offers access to AI tools and provides policies to help instructors and staff determine which tools are acceptable for different types of student data.

Penn requires all community members (educators, staff, researchers, and students) to be transparent about the use of AI and to disclose when a work product was created wholly or partially using an AI tool.

Penn provides several licensed AI tools to its community, including Copilot Chat (Basic, free), Adobe Express (free), ChatGPT-EDU (purchase required), M365 Copilot Premium (purchase required), Gemini for Google Workspace (purchase required), Google NotebookLM (purchase required), Grammarly Pro (purchase required), Snowflake Data Analytics (purchase required), and Zoom AI Companion (free).
Users of AI at Penn are accountable for AI-generated content and should validate its accuracy with trusted first-party sources, being wary of misinformation or hallucinations.

Penn users should not input moderate or high-risk Penn data (per the Penn Data Risk Classification) or intellectual property into AI tools without careful consideration of data use policies, a protective contract, and review by Penn's Privacy Office and Office of Information Security.

It is not permissible under HIPAA or Penn Medicine policy to share patient or research participant information with open or public AI tools and services such as ChatGPT; individual patient data and data sets (even if deidentified) may not be exposed to such tools absent institutional approval.

Penn researchers should obtain IRB approvals prior to exposing research participant data to AI tools and should exercise caution when research involves high-risk data including PII and health information.

Penn's Office of Audit, Compliance & Privacy mandates that users of publicly available (unlicensed) AI tools must not enter any information that could identify a student, including names, ID numbers, email addresses, or detailed descriptions of student work or engagement that could be identifiable to others.

Penn mandates that student work (papers, projects) must not be entered into unlicensed AI tools without the student's permission, even if anonymized, because this work is part of the student's confidential academic record.

Instructors must not require students to enter their own work into unlicensed AI tools or use such tools in assignments; unlicensed tools may be used optionally by students at the instructor's discretion, but Penn-licensed tools should be used for mandatory coursework components.
Individual instructors at Penn determine their own policies related to acceptable student use of generative AI in coursework.

Penn community members should avoid uploading confidential or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize intellectual property rights.
University business processes using AI should have oversight, review, and verification of AI outputs in place to ensure reliability, consistency, and accuracy.

Penn educators should provide students with clear guidelines on the use of AI within coursework and should disclose to students when course materials have been created with AI or when AI detection software will be used.

In the absence of other guidance, Penn students should treat the use of AI as they would treat assistance from another person — if it is unacceptable to have another person substantially complete a task like writing an essay, it is also unacceptable to have AI complete the task.
Penn researchers should consult with department leadership and their discipline's publishing standards to determine how AI use should be accounted for with regard to authorship in publications.

At Wharton Academy, AI-generated work should be cited like any other reference material, including how and where students used AI-generated information; using AI-generated work without crediting the source is considered plagiarism.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from using AI to complete personal reflection or opinion-based tasks, from using AI to complete group assignments instead of collaborating with peers, and from using AI to cheat on exams or tests.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from directly copying answers from generative AI tools and submitting them as their own, from using AI to paraphrase or rewrite plagiarized content, and from posting AI-generated discussion posts within course community forums.

Wharton Academy permits students to use generative AI for brainstorming, learning efficiency, getting prompts, exploring different perspectives, asking for templates, getting preliminary feedback on written work, and language translation, at the discretion of faculty and instructional teams.

claimChanges.claimText: Claude Anthropic is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn’s Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) maintains updated institutional guidance on Penn-licensed AI tools, providing community access to PennChat (with free daily token allotments for FERPA-protected educational records and HIPAA-protected health information via PennKey while on campus or VPN), alongside Anthropic Enterprise (Claude), Articulate AI Assistant, Adobe Express, and Copilot Chat, while mandating that instructors must not require students to enter personal information or intellectual property into unlicensed tools.

Penn's Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning and Innovation (CETLI) instructs faculty that in all cases they should not upload student work into AI detectors, stating that uploading student work without consent violates FERPA and Penn privacy policies, and noting that AI detectors are not accurate enough to serve as evidence of misconduct due to frequent bias.

Google NotebookLM is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft M365 Copilot (Premium) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft Copilot Chat (Basic) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Snowflake Data Analytics Platform & Consulting is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.
PennChat (Pilot) is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Grammarly for Education is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Gemini for Google Workspace is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

ChatGPT Edu is listed for University of Pennsylvania in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Penn's CETLI generative AI guidance page was updated from referring to 'Penn AI Guidance and Policies' to 'Penn AI Tools and Policies', adding that Penn offers access to AI tools and provides policies to help instructors and staff determine which tools are acceptable for different types of student data.

Penn requires all community members (educators, staff, researchers, and students) to be transparent about the use of AI and to disclose when a work product was created wholly or partially using an AI tool.

Penn provides several licensed AI tools to its community, including Copilot Chat (Basic, free), Adobe Express (free), ChatGPT-EDU (purchase required), M365 Copilot Premium (purchase required), Gemini for Google Workspace (purchase required), Google NotebookLM (purchase required), Grammarly Pro (purchase required), Snowflake Data Analytics (purchase required), and Zoom AI Companion (free).
Users of AI at Penn are accountable for AI-generated content and should validate its accuracy with trusted first-party sources, being wary of misinformation or hallucinations.

Penn users should not input moderate or high-risk Penn data (per the Penn Data Risk Classification) or intellectual property into AI tools without careful consideration of data use policies, a protective contract, and review by Penn's Privacy Office and Office of Information Security.

It is not permissible under HIPAA or Penn Medicine policy to share patient or research participant information with open or public AI tools and services such as ChatGPT; individual patient data and data sets (even if deidentified) may not be exposed to such tools absent institutional approval.

Penn researchers should obtain IRB approvals prior to exposing research participant data to AI tools and should exercise caution when research involves high-risk data including PII and health information.

Penn's Office of Audit, Compliance & Privacy mandates that users of publicly available (unlicensed) AI tools must not enter any information that could identify a student, including names, ID numbers, email addresses, or detailed descriptions of student work or engagement that could be identifiable to others.

Penn mandates that student work (papers, projects) must not be entered into unlicensed AI tools without the student's permission, even if anonymized, because this work is part of the student's confidential academic record.

Instructors must not require students to enter their own work into unlicensed AI tools or use such tools in assignments; unlicensed tools may be used optionally by students at the instructor's discretion, but Penn-licensed tools should be used for mandatory coursework components.
Individual instructors at Penn determine their own policies related to acceptable student use of generative AI in coursework.

Penn community members should avoid uploading confidential or proprietary information to AI platforms prior to seeking patent or copyright protection, as doing so could jeopardize intellectual property rights.
University business processes using AI should have oversight, review, and verification of AI outputs in place to ensure reliability, consistency, and accuracy.

Penn educators should provide students with clear guidelines on the use of AI within coursework and should disclose to students when course materials have been created with AI or when AI detection software will be used.

In the absence of other guidance, Penn students should treat the use of AI as they would treat assistance from another person — if it is unacceptable to have another person substantially complete a task like writing an essay, it is also unacceptable to have AI complete the task.
Penn researchers should consult with department leadership and their discipline's publishing standards to determine how AI use should be accounted for with regard to authorship in publications.

At Wharton Academy, AI-generated work should be cited like any other reference material, including how and where students used AI-generated information; using AI-generated work without crediting the source is considered plagiarism.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from using AI to complete personal reflection or opinion-based tasks, from using AI to complete group assignments instead of collaborating with peers, and from using AI to cheat on exams or tests.

Wharton Academy prohibits students from directly copying answers from generative AI tools and submitting them as their own, from using AI to paraphrase or rewrite plagiarized content, and from posting AI-generated discussion posts within course community forums.

Wharton Academy permits students to use generative AI for brainstorming, learning efficiency, getting prompts, exploring different perspectives, asking for templates, getting preliminary feedback on written work, and language translation, at the discretion of faculty and instructional teams.
